L9: 
L10: The `node:fs` module enables interacting with the file system in a
L11: way modeled on standard POSIX functions.
L12: 
L13: To use the promise-based APIs:
L14: 
L15: ```mjs
L16: import * as fs from 'node:fs/promises';
L17: ```
L18: 
L19: ```cjs
L20: const fs = require('node:fs/promises');
L21: ```
L22: 
L23: To use the callback and sync APIs:
L24: 
L25: ```mjs
L26: import * as fs from 'node:fs';
L27: ```
L28: 
L29: ```cjs
L30: const fs = require('node:fs');
L31: ```
L32: All file system operations have synchronous, callback, and promise-based
L33: forms, and are accessible using both CommonJS syntax and ES6 Modules (ESM).
L34: ## Promise example
L35: 
L36: Promise-based operations return a promise that is fulfilled when the
L37: asynchronous operation is complete.
L38: 
L39: ```mjs
L40: import { unlink } from 'node:fs/promises';
L41: 
L42: try {
L43:   await unlink('/tmp/hello');
L44:   console.log('successfully deleted /tmp/hello');
L45: } catch (error) {
L46:   console.error('there was an error:', error.message);
L47: }
L48: ```
L49: 
L50: ```cjs
L51: const { unlink } = require('node:fs/promises');
L52: (async function(path) {
L53:   try {
L54:     await unlink(path);
L55:     console.log(`successfully deleted ${path}`);
L56:   } catch (error) {
L57:     console.error('there was an error:', error.message);
L58:   }
L59: })('/tmp/hello');
L60: ```
L61: ## Callback example
L62: 
L63: The callback form takes a completion callback function as its last
L64: argument and invokes the operation asynchronously. The arguments passed to
L65: the completion callback depend on the method, but the first argument is always
L66: reserved for an exception. If the operation is completed successfully, then
L67: the first argument is `null` or `undefined`.
L68: 
L69: ```mjs
L70: import { unlink } from 'node:fs';
L71: unlink('/tmp/hello', (err) => {
L72:   if (err) throw err;
L73:   console.log('successfully deleted /tmp/hello');
L74: });
L75: ```
L76: 
L77: ```cjs
L78: const { unlink } = require('node:fs');
L79: 
L80: unlink('/tmp/hello', (err) => {
L81:   if (err) throw err;
L82:   console.log('successfully deleted /tmp/hello');
L83: });
L84: ```
L85: 
L86: The callback-based versions of the `node:fs` module APIs are preferable over
L87: the use of the promise APIs when maximal performance (both in terms of
L88: execution time and memory allocation) is required.
L89: ## Synchronous example
L90: 
L91: The synchronous APIs block the Node.js event loop and further JavaScript
L92: execution until the operation is complete. Exceptions are thrown immediately
L93: and can be handled using `try…catch`, or can be allowed to bubble up.
L94: 
L95: ```mjs
L96: import { unlinkSync } from 'node:fs';
L97: 
L98: try {
L99:   unlinkSync('/tmp/hello');
L100:   console.log('successfully deleted /tmp/hello');
L101: } catch (err) {
L102:   // handle the error
L103: }
L104: ```
L105: 
L106: ```cjs
L107: const { unlinkSync } = require('node:fs');
L108: try {
L109:   unlinkSync('/tmp/hello');
L110:   console.log('successfully deleted /tmp/hello');
L111: } catch (err) {
L112:   // handle the error
L113: }
L114: ```
L115: ## Promises API
L116: 
L117: <!-- YAML
L118: added: v10.0.0
L119: changes:
L120:   - version: v14.0.0
L121:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/31553
L122:     description: Exposed as `require('fs/promises')`.
L123:   - version:
L124:     - v11.14.0
L125:     - v10.17.0
L126:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/26581
L127:     description: This API is no longer experimental.
L128:   - version: v10.1.0
L129:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/20504
L130:     description: The API is accessible via `require('fs').promises` only.
L131: -->
L132: The `fs/promises` API provides asynchronous file system methods that return
L133: promises.
L134: 
L135: The promise APIs use the underlying Node.js threadpool to perform file
L136: system operations off the event loop thread. These operations are not
L137: synchronized or threadsafe. Care must be taken when performing multiple
L138: concurrent modifications on the same file or data corruption may occur.
L139: ### Class: `FileHandle`
L140: 
L141: <!-- YAML
L142: added: v10.0.0
L143: -->
L144: 
L145: A {FileHandle} object is an object wrapper for a numeric file descriptor.
L146: 
L147: Instances of the {FileHandle} object are created by the `fsPromises.open()`
L148: method.
L149: 
L150: All {FileHandle} objects are {EventEmitter}s.
L151: If a {FileHandle} is not closed using the `filehandle.close()` method, it will
L152: try to automatically close the file descriptor and emit a process warning,
L153: helping to prevent memory leaks. Please do not rely on this behavior because
L154: it can be unreliable and the file may not be closed. Instead, always explicitly
L155: close {FileHandle}s. Node.js may change this behavior in the future.
L156: #### Event: `'close'`
L157: 
L158: <!-- YAML
L159: added: v15.4.0
L160: -->
L161: 
L162: The `'close'` event is emitted when the {FileHandle} has been closed and can no
L163: longer be used.
L164: #### `filehandle.appendFile(data[, options])`
L165: <!-- YAML
L166: added: v10.0.0
L167: changes:
L168:   - version:
L169:     - v21.1.0
L170:     - v20.10.0
L171:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/50095
L172:     description: The `flush` option is now supported.
L173:   - version:
L174:       - v15.14.0
L175:       - v14.18.0
L176:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/37490
L177:     description: The `data` argument supports `AsyncIterable`, `Iterable`, and `Stream`.
L178:   - version: v14.0.0
L179:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/31030
L180:     description: The `data` parameter won't coerce unsupported input to
L181:                  strings anymore.
L182: -->
L183: * `data` {string|Buffer|TypedArray|DataView|AsyncIterable|Iterable|Stream}
L184: * `options` {Object|string}
L185:   * `encoding` {string|null} **Default:** `'utf8'`
L186:   * `signal` {AbortSignal|undefined} allows aborting an in-progress writeFile. **Default:** `undefined`
L187: * Returns: {Promise} Fulfills with `undefined` upon success.
L188: 
L189: Alias of [`filehandle.writeFile()`][].
L190: When operating on file handles, the mode cannot be changed from what it was set
L191: to with [`fsPromises.open()`][]. Therefore, this is equivalent to
L192: [`filehandle.writeFile()`][].

L215: #### `filehandle.close()`
L216: 
L217: <!-- YAML
L218: added: v10.0.0
L219: -->
L220: 
L221: * Returns: {Promise} Fulfills with `undefined` upon success.
L222: 
L223: Closes the file handle after waiting for any pending operation on the handle to
L224: complete.
L225: 
L226: ```mjs
L227: import { open } from 'node:fs/promises';
L228: 
L229: let filehandle;
L230: try {
L231:   filehandle = await open('thefile.txt', 'r');
L232: } finally {
L233:   await filehandle?.close();
L234: }
L235: ```
L236: #### `filehandle.createReadStream([options])`
L237: 
L238: <!-- YAML
L239: added: v16.11.0
L240: -->
L241: 
L242: * `options` {Object}
L243:   * `encoding` {string} **Default:** `null`
L244:   * `autoClose` {boolean} **Default:** `true`
L245:   * `emitClose` {boolean} **Default:** `true`
L246:   * `start` {integer}
L247:   * `end` {integer} **Default:** `Infinity`
L248:   * `highWaterMark` {integer} **Default:** `64 * 1024`
L249:   * `signal` {AbortSignal|undefined} **Default:** `undefined`
L250: * Returns: {fs.ReadStream}
L251: `options` can include `start` and `end` values to read a range of bytes from
L252: the file instead of the entire file. Both `start` and `end` are inclusive and
L253: start counting at 0, allowed values are in the
L254: \[0, [`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`][]] range. If `start` is
L255: omitted or `undefined`, `filehandle.createReadStream()` reads sequentially from
L256: the current file position. The `encoding` can be any one of those accepted by
L257: {Buffer}.
L258: If the `FileHandle` points to a character device that only supports blocking
L259: reads (such as keyboard or sound card), read operations do not finish until data
L260: is available. This can prevent the process from exiting and the stream from
L261: closing naturally.
L262: 
L263: By default, the stream will emit a `'close'` event after it has been
L264: destroyed.  Set the `emitClose` option to `false` to change this behavior.
L265: 
L266: ```mjs
L267: import { open } from 'node:fs/promises';
L268: const fd = await open('/dev/input/event0');
L269: // Create a stream from some character device.
L270: const stream = fd.createReadStream();
L271: setTimeout(() => {
L272:   stream.close(); // This may not close the stream.
L273:   // Artificially marking end-of-stream, as if the underlying resource had
L274:   // indicated end-of-file by itself, allows the stream to close.
L275:   // This does not cancel pending read operations, and if there is such an
L276:   // operation, the process may still not be able to exit successfully
L277:   // until it finishes.
L278:   stream.push(null);
L279:   stream.read(0);
L280: }, 100);
L281: ```
L282: If `autoClose` is false, then the file descriptor won't be closed, even if
L283: there's an error. It is the application's responsibility to close it and make
L284: sure there's no file descriptor leak. If `autoClose` is set to true (default
L285: behavior), on `'error'` or `'end'` the file descriptor will be closed
L286: automatically.
L287: 
L288: An example to read the last 10 bytes of a file which is 100 bytes long:
L289: 
L290: ```mjs
L291: import { open } from 'node:fs/promises';
L292: const fd = await open('sample.txt');
L293: fd.createReadStream({ start: 90, end: 99 });
L294: ```
L295: #### `filehandle.createWriteStream([options])`
L296: 
L297: <!-- YAML
L298: added: v16.11.0
L299: changes:
L300:   - version:
L301:     - v21.0.0
L302:     - v20.10.0
L303:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/50093
L304:     description: The `flush` option is now supported.
L305: -->
L306: * `options` {Object}
L307:   * `encoding` {string} **Default:** `'utf8'`
L308:   * `autoClose` {boolean} **Default:** `true`
L309:   * `emitClose` {boolean} **Default:** `true`
L310:   * `start` {integer}
L311:   * `highWaterMark` {number} **Default:** `16384`
L312:   * `flush` {boolean} If `true`, the underlying file descriptor is flushed
L313:     prior to closing it. **Default:** `false`.
L314: * Returns: {fs.WriteStream}
L315: `options` may also include a `start` option to allow writing data at some
L316: position past the beginning of the file, allowed values are in the
L317: \[0, [`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`][]] range. Modifying a file rather than
L318: replacing it may require the `flags` `open` option to be set to `r+` rather than
L319: the default `r`. The `encoding` can be any one of those accepted by {Buffer}.
L320: If `autoClose` is set to true (default behavior) on `'error'` or `'finish'`
L321: the file descriptor will be closed automatically. If `autoClose` is false,
L322: then the file descriptor won't be closed, even if there's an error.
L323: It is the application's responsibility to close it and make sure there's no
L324: file descriptor leak.
L325: 
L326: By default, the stream will emit a `'close'` event after it has been
L327: destroyed.  Set the `emitClose` option to `false` to change this behavior.
L328: #### `filehandle.datasync()`
L329: 
L330: <!-- YAML
L331: added: v10.0.0
L332: -->
L333: 
L334: * Returns: {Promise} Fulfills with `undefined` upon success.
L335: 
L336: Forces all currently queued I/O operations associated with the file to the
L337: operating system's synchronized I/O completion state. Refer to the POSIX
L338: fdatasync(2) documentation for details.
L339: 
L340: Unlike `filehandle.sync` this method does not flush modified metadata.

L438: #### `filehandle.readableWebStream([options])`

L440: added: v17.0.0
L441: changes:
L442:   - version: v22.17.0
L443:     pr-url: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/57513
L444:     description: Marking the API stable.
L445:   - version: v22.17.0

L462: Returns a byte-oriented `ReadableStream` that may be used to read the file's
L463: contents.
L464: 
L465: An error will be thrown if this method is called more than once or is called
L466: after the `FileHandle` is closed or closing.
L467: 
L468: ```mjs
L469: import {
L470:   open,
L471: } from 'node:fs/promises';
L472:

L474: for await (const chunk of file.readableWebStream())
L475:   console.log(chunk);
L476: 
L477: await file.close();
L478: ```

L481: const {
L482:   open,
L483: } = require('node:fs/promises');
L484: 
L485: (async () => {
L486:   const file = await open('./some/file/to/read');
L487: 
L488:   for await (const chunk of file.readableWebStream())

L498: #### `filehandle.readFile(options)`
L499: 
L500: <!-- YAML
L501: added: v10.0.0
L502: -->
L503: 
L504: * `options` {Object|string}
L505:   * `encoding` {string|null} **Default:** `null`
L506:   * `signal` {AbortSignal} allows aborting an in-progress readFile
L507: * Returns: {Promise} Fulfills upon a successful read with the contents of the
L508:   file. If no encoding is specified (using `options.encoding`), the data is
L509:   returned as a {Buffer} object. Otherwise, the data will be a string.
L510: 
L511: Asynchronously reads the entire contents of a file.
L512: If `options` is a string, then it specifies the `encoding`.
L513: 
L514: The {FileHandle} has to support reading.
L515: 
L516: If one or more `filehandle.read()` calls are made on a file handle and then a
L517: `filehandle.readFile()` call is made, the data will be read from the current
L518: position till the end of the file. It doesn't always read from the beginning
L519: of the file.

L12: ## NAME         cite15†top L13: 
L14:            read - read from a file descriptor
L15: ## LIBRARY         cite15†top L16: 
L17:            Standard C library (libc, -lc)
L18: 
L19: 
L20: ## SYNOPSIS         cite15†top L21: 
L22:            #include <unistd.h>
L23: 
L24:            ssize_t read(size_t count;
L25:                         int fd, void buf[count], size_t count);
L26: ## DESCRIPTION         cite15†top L27: 
L28:            read() attempts to read up to count bytes from file descriptor fd
L29:            into the buffer starting at buf.
L30: 
L31:            On files that support seeking, the read operation commences at the
L32:            file offset, and the file offset is incremented by the number of
L33:            bytes read.  If the file offset is at or past the end of file, no
L34:            bytes are read, and read() returns zero.
L35:            If count is zero, read() may detect the errors described below.
L36:            In the absence of any errors, or if read() does not check for
L37:            errors, a read() with a count of 0 returns zero and has no other
L38:            effects.
L39: 
L40:            According to POSIX.1, if count is greater than SSIZE_MAX, the
L41:            result is implementation-defined; see NOTES for the upper limit on
L42:            Linux.
L43: ## RETURN VALUE         cite15†top L44: 
L45:            On success, the number of bytes read is returned (zero indicates
L46:            end of file), and the file position is advanced by this number.
L47:            It is not an error if this number is smaller than the number of
L48:            bytes requested; this may happen for example because fewer bytes
L49:            are actually available right now (maybe because we were close to
L50:            end-of-file, or because we are reading from a pipe, or from a
L51:            terminal), or because read() was interrupted by a signal.  See
L52:            also NOTES.
L53: 
L54:            On error, -1 is returned, and cite16†errno is set to indicate the error.
L55:            In this case, it is left unspecified whether the file position (if
L56:            any) changes.
L57: ## ERRORS         cite15†top L58: 
L59:            EAGAIN The file descriptor fd refers to a file other than a socket
L60:                   and has been marked nonblocking (O_NONBLOCK), and the read
L61:                   would block.  See cite17†open(2) for further details on the
L62:                   O_NONBLOCK flag.
L63: 
L64:            EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK
L65:                   The file descriptor fd refers to a socket and has been
L66:                   marked nonblocking (O_NONBLOCK), and the read would block.
L67:                   POSIX.1-2001 allows either error to be returned for this
L68:                   case, and does not require these constants to have the same
L69:                   value, so a portable application should check for both
L70:                   possibilities.
L71: 
L72:            EBADF  fd is not a valid file descriptor or is not open for
L73:                   reading.
L74: 
L75:            EFAULT buf is outside your accessible address space.
L76: 
L77:            EINTR  The call was interrupted by a signal before any data was
L78:                   read; see cite18†signal(7) .
L79: 
L80:            EINVAL fd is attached to an object which is unsuitable for
L81:                   reading; or the file was opened with the O_DIRECT flag, and
L82:                   either the address specified in buf, the value specified in
L83:                   count, or the file offset is not suitably aligned.
L84: 
L85:            EINVAL fd was created via a call to cite19†timerfd_create(2) and the
L86:                   wrong size buffer was given to read(); see
L87:                   cite19†timerfd_create(2) for further information.
L88: 
L89:            EIO    I/O error.  This will happen for example when the process
L90:                   is in a background process group, tries to read from its
L91:                   controlling terminal, and either it is ignoring or blocking
L92:                   SIGTTIN or its process group is orphaned.  It may also
L93:                   occur when there is a low-level I/O error while reading
L94:                   from a disk or tape.  A further possible cause of EIO on
L95:                   networked filesystems is when an advisory lock had been
L96:                   taken out on the file descriptor and this lock has been
L97:                   lost.  See the Lost locks section of cite20†fcntl(2) for further
L98:                   details.
L99: 
L100:            EISDIR fd refers to a directory.
L101: 
L102:            Other errors may occur, depending on the object connected to fd.
L103: ## STANDARDS         cite15†top L104: 
L105:            POSIX.1-2008.
L106: 
L107: 
L108: ## HISTORY         cite15†top L109: 
L110:            SVr4, 4.3BSD, POSIX.1-2001.
L111: ## NOTES         cite15†top L112: 
L113:            On Linux, read() (and similar system calls) will transfer at most
L114:            0x7ffff000 (2,147,479,552) bytes, returning the number of bytes
L115:            actually transferred.  (This is true on both 32-bit and 64-bit
L116:            systems.)
L117: 
L118:            On NFS filesystems, reading small amounts of data will update the
L119:            timestamp only the first time, subsequent calls may not do so.
L120:            This is caused by client side attribute caching, because most if
L121:            not all NFS clients leave st_atime (last file access time) updates
L122:            to the server, and client side reads satisfied from the client's
L123:            cache will not cause st_atime updates on the server as there are
L124:            no server-side reads.  UNIX semantics can be obtained by disabling
L125:            client-side attribute caching, but in most situations this will
L126:            substantially increase server load and decrease performance.
L127: ## BUGS         cite15†top L128: 
L129:            According to POSIX.1-2008/SUSv4 Section XSI 2.9.7 ("Thread
L130:            Interactions with Regular File Operations"):
L131: 
L132:                All of the following functions shall be atomic with respect to
L133:                each other in the effects specified in POSIX.1-2008 when they
L134:                operate on regular files or symbolic links: ...
L135: 
L136:            Among the APIs subsequently listed are read() and cite21†readv(2) .  And
L137:            among the effects that should be atomic across threads (and
L138:            processes) are updates of the file offset.  However, before Linux
L139:            3.14, this was not the case: if two processes that share an open
L140:            file description (see cite17†open(2) ) perform a read() (or cite21†readv(2) ) at
L141:            the same time, then the I/O operations were not atomic with
L142:            respect to updating the file offset, with the result that the
L143:            reads in the two processes might (incorrectly) overlap in the
L144:            blocks of data that they obtained.  This problem was fixed in
L145:            Linux 3.14.
